page.text:
The complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ arise through the algebraic completion of the real
continuum $\mathbb{R}$. While the real numbers resolve all topological deficiencies
via Cauchy completeness, they remain algebraically incomplete: the quadratic equation
$x^2 + 1 = 0$ admits no solution among real magnitudes. By formally adjoining an
ideal element $i$—the imaginary unit satisfying $i^2 = -1$—we obtain the quotient ring
$\mathbb{R}[t]/(t^2 + 1)$, which is a field because the quadratic polynomial $t^2 + 1$
is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$.

Alternatively, following William Rowan Hamilton (1835), the complex numbers can be
constructed purely constructively as pairs of real numbers $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$
equipped with the componentwise addition $(x_1, y_1) + (x_2, y_2) = (x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2)$
and the twisted multiplication $(x_1, y_1) \cdot (x_2, y_2) = (x_1 x_2 - y_1 y_2, \, x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1)$.
This construction entirely demystifies 'imaginary' quantities, embedding the real numbers
isomorphically as the horizontal axis $x \mapsto (x, 0)$ and identifying $i = (0, 1)$ so
that $(0, 1) \cdot (0, 1) = (-1, 0) = -1$.

The resulting field $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed (the Fundamental Theorem of
Algebra) and simultaneously inherits the two-dimensional Euclidean topology of
$\mathbb{R}^2$, synthesizing algebra, geometry, and analysis into a unified whole.
